Build a payment processing platform that stores cardholder data, runs PCI-DSS compliant tokenization, settles funds to merchant bank accounts, and produces an immutable audit trail of every financial transaction.

Build an integrated healthcare claims and revenue-cycle platform for a network of hospitals, outpatient clinics, and partner pharmacies, used by clinicians, billing staff, compliance officers, and external insurance adjusters. The platform ingests patient medical records and PHI from EHR and EMR systems, captures clinical diagnosis codes, prescription histories, and lab results, and reconciles each encounter against the relevant insurance claim policies under HIPAA. It must also run the downstream financial settlement: posting charges, processing patient payments that include cardholder data under PCI-DSS, reconciling insurer remittances, and supporting payroll for clinical staff under SOX-style financial controls. Every clinical and financial action needs an immutable audit trail, encryption at rest for all PHI and cardholder data, and fine-grained role-based access for doctors, nurses, billing clerks, auditors, and adjusters, with break-glass emergency access that is itself fully audited. The product has to integrate with pharmacy benefit managers, government regulatory reporting endpoints, clearinghouses, and banking settlement rails, and expose a patient-facing portal where people can view their diagnoses, prescriptions, claim status, and outstanding balances. Clinicians need order entry, e-prescribing with drug-interaction checks, and documentation workflows that feed coding; billing teams need charge capture, claim scrubbing, denial management, appeals tracking, and remittance posting; compliance officers need configurable retention policies, legal holds, and exportable audit reports for regulators. The system must support multi-facility tenancy with per-facility configuration, eligibility verification against payer APIs, prior-authorization workflows, and reconciliation of partial and bundled payments across encounters. There are several areas the team has not fully pinned down yet: the exact compliance scope is somewhat undecided and may possibly expand to GDPR and FERPA depending on the deployment region, the data-retention windows for clinical versus financial records are tbd, the dispute-resolution rules for denied or partially paid claims are not sure yet, and the fraud-detection thresholds for suspicious financial transactions still need to be determined. The roadmap also gestures at biometric login, analytics dashboards for utilization and denial trends, automated regulatory exports, configurable approval chains, and delegated administration, among various other things like clinical decision support and population-health reporting that may or may not land in the first release. The goal is a single regulated system of record that keeps clinical care, insurance reconciliation, and financial settlement consistent, auditable, and compliant end to end across every participating facility, payer, and downstream integration partner in the network, while remaining performant under heavy concurrent load and resilient to the failure of any single integration or regional data center. Operationally the platform must run as a multi-region deployment with disaster recovery, point-in-time restore of clinical and financial data, and tenant-level data isolation so that one facility's PHI is never visible to another. Observability, anomaly alerting on claim and payment patterns, and a documented incident-response process for suspected PHI or cardholder-data breaches are required, along with periodic access recertification for every privileged role. Finally, the team wants an extensible policy engine so that new payer rules, regulatory mandates, and reconciliation edge cases can be configured rather than hard-coded, since the regulatory landscape and payer contracts are expected to keep changing well after the initial launch.
